catalog_quote: Urdu stress is sensitive to syllable weight. This weight can be represented by moraic count of each syllable [7]. ... long vowels are bi-moriac and short vowels are mono-moraic in Urdu. In addition, each coda consonant has a weight equivalent to a single mora [4], [9]. ... Syllables can be mono-moraic (light), bi-moraic (heavy) and tri-moraic (super-heavy, e.g. closed syllables with long vowels). ... Analysis shows that heavy and super-heavy syllables may take primary or secondary stress. Primary stress is assigned to the first bi-moraic or tri-moraic syllables from the end of the word. Light syllables do not take stress. However, final syllables do not take stress even if they are heavy, indicating that the final mora is extrametrical [4]. sweep_summary: Three title hits, all already in the per-language bibliography. (1) Butt/Jabeen/Bögel 2016 (Linguistic Analysis 40) is sentence-level wh-phrase prosody, not word stress; paywalled (journal sells the article, no DOI, KOPS record metadata-only, ResearchGate 403); low priority. (2) Hussain 1997 Northwestern dissertation, which earlier passes recorded as 'not online', IS online at the CLE URL that Glottolog itself lists (https://www.cle.org.pk/Publication/theses/1997/phonetic_correlates.pdf); downloaded (5.95 MB UMI scan, no text), scanned the front matter and the stress chapter (diss. pp. 39-52) one page at a time, and read the rule first-hand: final mora extrametrical, rightmost heavy syllable stressed, final syllable only if super-heavy, penult if all light, one stress per word, 'fixed stress.. weakly variable'. (3) Hussain 2007 is the UMI reprint of the same dissertation (Glottolog note), so a duplicate. The 1997 statement confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and refines it by dropping the hedge; the current deciding source (Hussain 2005) is the author's later revision adding secondary stresses. Semantic Scholar could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.quote: Generalizing over all words, if a final syllable belongs to {super-heavy} it is stressed, and if it belongs to {light, heavy} it is not stressed. If a final syllable is not super-heavy, the syllable belonging to {heavy, super-heavy} closest to the end of the word is stressed. And if the final syllable is not super-heavy and there are no syllables belonging to {heavy, super-heavy} preceding the final syllable, the penultimate syllable is stressed. [p. 50:] The whole stress algorithm can then be simplified into the statement that the last heavy syllable is stressed (syllable weights counted after subtracting away the extrametricality effect in the final syllable). If all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed.

new_statements.reading: Text is scanned of a UMI scan (one '}' and 'last' were scanned-garbled and are restored here; everything else verbatim). Urdu word stress is quantity-sensitive and unbounded, assigned right-to-left: with the final mora extrametrical, the rightmost heavy (multi-moraic) syllable is stressed; a final syllable takes stress only when super-heavy (VVC/VCC); if no syllable is heavy, default is the penult. One stress per word (p. 51); author calls it 'a fixed stress language' with 'signs of being a weakly variable stress language' (a few grammatically related minimal pairs, p. 50). Evidence base: dictionary stress marks (Qureshi 1992) over all licensed 2-3 syllable weight templates. This is consistent with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and removes the hedge: the multiple-stress / speaker-variation caveats come only from the author's later 2005 conference paper (the current deciding source), which keeps the same primary-stress rule but adds secondary stresses per morpheme from informal Lahore speaker feedback (Jabeen 2019 diss. pp. 44-45 criticizes that addition). Recommend citing the 1997 dissertation as the primary statement (rightmost heavy with final-mora extrametricality, else penult) and keeping Hussain 2005 as a note on secondary stress and variation.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Urdu depends on syllable weight, and has been explored by Hussain (2004), who proposed an Urdu phonological stress-marking algorithm. This algorithm classifies Urdu syllables as either monomoraic, bimoraic, or trimoraic. Given these definitions, the algorithm states that a trimoraic (i.e., super-heavy) syllable in final position is stressed; if the final syllable is not trimoraic, then the rightmost non-final bimoraic (i.e., heavy) or trimoraic (i.e., super-heavy) syllable is stressed; and if all syllables are monomoraic (i.e., light), the penultimate syllable is stressed. The stressed syllable attracts a pitch accent.

Hussain (2004) in the re…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Hussain 1997 statement (rightmost heavy with the final syllable counting only when super-heavy, else penult): the paper simply restates Hussain's algorithm in mora terms. It adds the pitch accent/AP domain (one pitch accent per AP anchored on the stressed syllable) and the caveat that pitch accent floats in all-light words. It says nothing about the secondary stresses or speaker variation of Hussain 2005, so it neither supports nor rejects them.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, right-to-left, unbounded: a final super-heavy (trimoraic) syllable is stressed; otherwise the rightmost non-final heavy or super-heavy syllable; if every syllable is light, the penult. The stressed syllable is the docking site of the pitch accent (p. 7: 'Pitch accents are those tones that attach to the stressed syllables (Hussain, 1997), and can be either low L*, high H*, or rising L*+H.'). The authors' own transcriptions follow the rule: /ˈnəzər/ 'vision' (all light, penult), /nəˈmɑːz/ 'prayer' (final super-heavy), /ɡɪɽɡɪˈɽɑːneː/ 'lament' (rightmost non-final heavy), /ˈdʒoːhər ʃəˈnɑːs/ (pp. 7-8). The rule is attributed to Hussain (2004), the letter-to-sound paper for the Urdu TTS system, not stated from the authors' own data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; one stress per word is implicit in the AP model (one pitch accent per accentual phrase, which is 'a pitch bearing unit on a single word' or a small cluster, abstract and section 4.1).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 4, sentence following the quoted passage: 'If all the syllables are light, any syllable in a word can get a pitch accent independent of syllable status as stressed or unstressed.' — i.e. in all-light words the pitch accent is not tied to the (penultimate) stressed syllable. Case clitics, izāfat, conjunctive vāo, complex postpositions and complex verbs are folded into one AP with the host (abstract; pp. 9-11).
new_statements.identity_note: Urooj et al. 2019 is based on read speech of Pakistani (Lahore, Al-Khawarizmi Institute/CLE) Urdu speakers and restates the stress rule from Hussain's Urdu TTS work, i.e. standard Pakistani Urdu; no dialect qualification is given. Butt 1993 is the author's own Lahore-based Urdu. No work opened describes another variety.

tone_statements.quote: The basic phrasal accent in Urdu/Hindi has been established to be some form of LH, where the H functions as a boundary tone for the accentual phrase [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. We follow [4] and [5] in positing L*H as the basic phrasal accent. … Generally it seems that each content word receives an AP and each AP is characterized by an L*H with the H indicating the right boundary. … [1, 3] and [4] associate an L tone with a stressed syllable followed by phrasal tone (Ha) … We therefore adopt the L*H analysis.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2661, sec. 1 Introduction and sec. 2.1 Urdu/Hindi Intonation and Word Order
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone is posited: pitch is post-lexical intonation, each content word forming an accentual phrase with an L*H rise (L* on the stressed syllable, H a right-edge boundary tone).

sources.quote: p. 50 (scanned): "If the extrametricality is taken into account, the super-heavy/heavy distinction becomes a heavy/light distinction in final syllable. The whole stress algorithm can then be simplified into the statement that the last heavy syllable is stressed (syllable weights counted after subtracting away the extrametricality effect in the final syllable). sources.quote: As per the Centre for research in the Urdu language processing claims that “Urdu establishes a stress distinction involving weight of syllable. Hence Urdu can be termed as quantity sensitive language” (Nayyar, 2017) However, it is noted that “Affixation seems to have stress assigning and stress removing property. [...] It is observed that in Urdu affix is treated separate from the root. Root has separate stress and affix may or may not bear stress.” Since the current paper is not exhaustive list of stress in Urdu it can be concluded that stress in Urdu is syllable timed and stress patterns are extremely different from the stress timed English language.

sources.quote: Urdu, on the other hand, is a syllable-timed language (Hussain, 1997) with little reduction (in vowel quality and duration) in unstressed syllables. Urdu has a phonological distinction between long and short vowels as well as consonants (Saleem-ud-Din & Anjum, 2013). This leads to minimal pairs in consonantal length [ˈpə.t̪ɑ] 'address' and [ˈpə.t̪ːɑ] 'leaf' and vocalic length [bin] 'without' and [biːn] 'flute'. Furthermore, Urdu is an edge-prominence language (Jabeen, 2019), where prominence is used to mark phrase edges instead of phrase heads. Jabeen and Delais-Roussarie (2020) have shown that Accentual Phrases in Urdu are produced with a rising f0 contour. [...] All the target nouns were bisyllabic trochaic words (ˈCVː.CV), followed by a monosyllabic accusative case marker ("ko").
sources.note: marginal: Focus marking by duration in Urdu speakers in Germany vs Pakistan; characterises Urdu as syllable-timed with edge-prominence marking, but is about sentence focus rather than word stress.

sources.citation: Ul Ain, Qurrat, Muhammad Asim Mahmood, Syed Muhammad Muslim Raza & Anam Zakir. 2023. An Acoustic Investigation of Primary and Secondary Lexical Stress of Urdu. GEMA Online Journal of Language Studies 23(1): 74-92. doi:10.17576/gema-2023-2301-05
sources.quote: The analysis reveals three levels of lexical stress: primary, secondary, and unstressed. Vowel duration is the strongest cue to correlate with the levels of stress in Urdu while stressed segments prone to have higher values of intensity. Overall, a trend of lower F0 and higher formant values could be seen against stressed syllables. [...] The first word 'pajama' has its primary stress on the penultimate syllable 'ja' that has the longest vowel duration, i.e., 104ms. Secondary stress falls on the final syllable 'ma' [...] The second word 'karkhana' also has three stress levels and the stress patterns change here with the syllable templates. The first syllable (CVVC) has the main stress with longest vowel duration (118ms) while the penultimate syllable has secondary stress (89ms) [...] The next target word is 'nasazgar' that has two super-heavy and one heavy syllable (CVV.CVVC.CVVC). The competition between the two super-heavy syllables is won by the final syllable
sources.note: Acoustic study of primary and secondary lexical stress in Urdu trisyllabic words (nine Lahore speakers): three stress levels found, vowel duration the strongest cue, intensity higher on stressed syllables, F0 lower on stressed syllables.

sources.quote: Hussain (1997, as cited in Dyrud, 1997) notes that when there are light syllables in a word string then the penultimate syllable is stressed and if final syllable is heavy, then the stress is assigned on final heavy. Urdu also exhibits extrametricality phenomenon, where the final mora carries no weight and is not counted in assigning the stress location. [...] Hussain argues that Urdu has lexical stress, which is often marked on a final heavy syllable. However, the final heavy syllable does not contribute to the weight of a final syllable because of extrametricality. Urdu is a fixed stress language since syllable weight determines the primary stress in a word.
sources.locator: p. 93 (Introduction / literature review); also p. 93: 'Urdu words are not differentiated regarding stress alone since stress is not distinct in Hindi-Urdu.'

sources.quote: 'Generally, the location of word stress in Hindi-Urdu is predictable on the basis of syllable weight. Probably the simplest account of stress placement in Hindi-Urdu comes from Hussain (1997). ... syllables can be classified as monomoraic or light (V), bimoraic or heavy (VV or VC), or trimoraic or superheavy (VVC or VCC). Given these definitions, Hussain (1997) explains that the last heavy syllable is stressed, and if all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed. This account assumes a notion of extrametricality, which says the final mora of the word is invisible to the stress
sources.note: Independent open carrier of Hussain 1997's placement rule (incl. penult default) plus a production/perception study of the stress minimal pairs; replaces the Wikipedia paraphrase in the screen chain.

sources.quote: The basic phrasal accent in Urdu/Hindi has been established to be some form of LH, where the H functions as a boundary tone for the accentual phrase [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. We follow [4] and [5] in positing L*H as the basic phrasal accent. … Generally it seems that each content word receives an AP and each AP is characterized by an L*H with the H indicating the right boundary. … [1, 3] and [4] associate an L tone with a stressed syllable followed by phrasal tone (Ha) … We therefore adopt the L*H analysis.
sources.locator: p. 2661, sec. 1 Introduction and sec. 2.1 Urdu/Hindi Intonation and Word Order
sources.note: No lexical tone is posited: pitch is post-lexical intonation, each content word forming an accentual phrase with an L*H rise (L* on the stressed syllable, H a right-edge boundary tone).

tone.quote: Les mots hindis ont une syllabe accentuée, dont la place dépend de la forme du mot. Lorsque les deux dernières syllabes du mot sont « légères » (V ou CV) ou « lourdes » (CVː, Vː, CVC ou VC), c'est l'avant-dernière syllabe qui est accentuée (1). Lorsque l'avant-dernière syllabe est légère, et que la dernière syllabe est lourde, l'accent est attiré sur cette syllabe (2). ex. (1) 'ʃaː.diː mariage, 'gaː.liː injure (2) ga.'li: ruelle, na.'hĩ: non [...] L'accent de mot est important en hindi, et fonction de la structure des syllabes.
tone.locator: p. 4, section 4 'Les autres objets de la langue' (accent statement; the sheet has no tone item)
tone.translation: Hindi words have one stressed syllable, whose place depends on the shape of the word. When the last two syllables of the word are both 'light' (V or CV) or both 'heavy' (CVV, VV, CVC or VC), it is the penultimate syllable that is stressed (1). When the penultimate syllable is light and the last syllable is heavy, the stress is attracted onto that syllable (2). ex. (1) 'shaa.dii 'marriage', 'gaa.lii 'insult' (2) ga.'lii 'lane', na.'hii 'no' [...] Word stress is important in Hindi, and depends on syllable structure.
